title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
summary: Fishermen and a group of schoolchildren on a research trip help marine biologists calmly guide a confused young whale back to the open sea.
poll: Helping a lost wild animal is always worth the time and effort.

versions.title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
versions.text:
One day, men went to sea. They went in a boat. They saw a big whale.

It was in shallow water. It swam in rings. It did not go to deep water.

The men thought it was lost. They called for help. Some helpers came fast.

The helpers know whales well. Some kids were there too. They came to learn.

They want to learn about the sea. The whale had lost its group. A group of whales is a pod.

It swam into the bay. That was a mistake. No one touched the whale.

A loud noise could scare it. They made a soft sound. The sound would guide it.

The boat moved out to sea. The sound helped guide the whale. The whale swam after it.

The kids just watched. They stayed calm. They made no noise.

At last, the whale swam out to sea. Other whales called to it. The whale found its pod!

The kids learned a good lesson. A lost one needs a calm hand. It does not need noise.

versions.title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
versions.text:
One morning, fishermen went out to sea. They went in a small boat. Near the shore, they saw a large whale.

It was swimming in shallow water. It kept swimming in circles. It did not swim out to deep water.

The fishermen thought the whale was lost. They called for help. Some helpers came fast.

The helpers knew whales well. Some children were there too. They came on a trip.

They wanted to learn about the sea. The whale had lost its pod. A pod is a group of whales.

This whale swam into the bay. It was a mistake. No one touched the whale.

A sudden, loud noise could scare it. So they made a slow, steady sound. The sound was meant to guide it.

The boat moved out toward deep water. The steady sound helped guide the whale. The whale began to follow the sound.

The children watched from a safe spot. They stayed calm the whole time.

After a while, the whale swam into deep water. The children heard other whales calling to it. The lost whale had found its pod!

The children learned an important lesson. A lost whale needs patience and gentle help. It does not need noise or rushing.

versions.title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
versions.text:
One quiet morning, fishermen went out to sea. Near the shore, they saw a large whale. It moved slowly through shallow water.

The whale kept swimming in tight circles. It did not head out to deep water. The fishermen thought it was lost.

They called for help on their radio. Marine helpers came fast. They knew a lot about whales.

That same morning, some children were nearby on a boat. They were on a trip to learn about the sea.

The helpers said young whales can lose their pod. A pod is the group of whales they travel with. This whale had swum into the bay by mistake.

The team did not touch the whale. A sudden, loud noise could scare it more. So they made a slow, steady, calm sound.

Carefully, the boat moved toward deep water. The steady sound helped guide the whale along. Slowly, the whale began to follow it.

The children watched from a safe spot. They stayed quiet and calm.

After almost an hour, the whale reached deep water at last. In the distance, the children heard other whales calling out. The lost whale had found its pod!

The children learned an important lesson that day. A frightened animal needs patience and gentle help, not noise.

versions.title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
versions.text:
One quiet morning, Captain Yusuf and his crew went out to sea. Near the shore, they saw a large whale. It moved slowly through shallow water, swimming alone.

The whale kept circling in the same spot. It did not head out to deep water. The fishermen worried it was lost and might get stuck.

Captain Yusuf called for help on his radio. Marine helpers came fast to the bay. They knew a lot about whales.

That same morning, some children were nearby on a boat with Dr. Huda, a marine helper. They were on a school trip.

Dr. Huda said young whales can lose their pod. A pod is the group of whales they travel with. This whale had swum into the bay by mistake.

The team did not touch the whale. A sudden, loud noise could scare it deeper into the bay. So they made a slow, steady sound with their engine to guide it.

Carefully, the boat moved toward deep water while the sound played on. Slowly, the whale began to turn and follow the sound that was meant to guide it.

The children watched quietly from a safe spot. They stayed calm so the whale would not feel more afraid.

After almost an hour of slow, patient work, the whale reached deep water. In the distance, everyone heard other whales calling out. The lost young whale had found its pod again!

The children learned an important lesson that day. A frightened animal needs patience and gentle help, never noise.

versions.title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
versions.text:
Just after sunrise, Captain Yusuf and his crew set out along the coast. Near the shoreline, they saw something odd. A large shape was circling slowly in the shallow water. It was a young whale, alone.

Instead of heading to open water, the whale kept turning in one small spot close to the coastline. The fishermen thought it was confused. They worried it might get stuck if the tide dropped.

Captain Yusuf called the research center for help. Within minutes, a team of marine helpers set out toward the bay.

That same morning, some schoolchildren were aboard the helpers' boat. They were there on a field trip to learn about the sea. Dr. Huda, the lead helper, explained what was happening.

Young whales usually travel with a pod, a family group. Sometimes a strong current or the noise of boats can separate a young whale from its pod. Then it gets confused about which way to swim.

Dr. Huda warned the team not to touch the whale. Sudden noise might scare it further. Instead, the team used their engine to make a slow, steady sound that whales find calming.

Carefully, the boat moved toward deeper water. The steady sound seemed to guide the whale along behind it. The children watched quietly, writing down notes for the helpers.

With patience, after nearly an hour, the whale reached the open sea. From far away, the children heard other whales calling back to it. The young whale had rejoined its pod.

versions.title: The Whale Who Lost Its Way
versions.text:
Just after sunrise, Captain Yusuf and his fishing crew set out along the Red Sea coast, as they did most mornings, scanning the water more out of habit than any real expectation of seeing something unusual. Near the shoreline, however, they noticed a large shape circling slowly through the shallow water, which turned out, on closer inspection, to be a young whale swimming alone and clearly disoriented.

Rather than heading toward open water, the whale continued turning within the same narrow stretch close to the coastline. Judging by its size, the fishermen estimated that it was no more than a year or two old, and they suspected that it could no longer navigate its way back toward deeper water on its own. Consequently, they worried it might become stranded should the tide continue dropping through the morning.

Captain Yusuf immediately radioed the coastal research center, and within minutes a rescue team of marine biologists, scientists who study whales and other marine creatures, set out toward the bay to investigate the unusual sighting.

That same morning, a group of schoolchildren happened to be aboard the biologists' research boat, learning about ocean life during a field trip. Dr. Huda, the lead biologist, calmly explained to the children what was happening as their boat slowly approached the circling whale, taking care not to startle it any further.

Young whales typically migrate alongside a pod, a family group that helps guide them along the coast during their long seasonal journeys. Occasionally, however, a strong current or the noise of passing vessels can separate a young whale from its pod, leaving it unable to navigate back toward the open sea with any confidence.

Dr. Huda warned the team against touching the whale or startling it with sudden, loud noise, since a frightened whale might panic and swim even farther into danger rather than toward safety. Instead, her team used the boat's engine to produce a slow, steady acoustic signal, a low rhythmic sound that whales often find calming rather than threatening, one that marine biologists worldwide rely on to guide lost whales back toward open water.

Carefully, the research boat moved toward deeper water, and the steady acoustic signal seemed to guide the whale along just behind it, almost as though the whale trusted the familiar rhythm more than the unfamiliar shallows surrounding it. The children watched quietly from a safe distance, recording careful notes so that the biologists could study the whale's behavior afterward and add the rescue to the center's long-term records.

With patience, after nearly an hour of slow, careful work, the whale finally reached open water. In the distance, everyone aboard could hear other whales calling back to it across the sea. The young whale had rejoined its pod at last, able once again to migrate safely along the coast, and the children aboard the rescue boat cheered quietly, proud of what patient, careful teamwork had accomplished that morning.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A fisherman catches a whale to sell its meat at the market in the town square
Fishermen and children help guide a lost young whale back to the deep sea
Children learn to swim and play safely alongside whales
Scientists study why whales grow to be so large and heavy
questions.why: The story centers on helping a confused young whale find its way back to deep water and its pod.

wrong.A: The whale is helped, not caught or sold.
wrong.C: The children do not swim with the whale.
wrong.D: The story is not about why whales are large.

questions.stem: Where did the fishermen first see the whale?
options: Far out in the deep sea where ships sail
In the shallow water near the shore
On the beach, resting far away from the water
Inside a fishing net left behind by sailors
questions.why: In the story, the fishermen saw the whale in shallow water.

wrong.A: The deep sea is where the whale should have been, not where it was seen.
wrong.C: The whale was in the water, not on the beach.
wrong.D: The whale was never caught in a net.

questions.stem: Why did the fishermen think the whale was lost?
options: It was swimming in circles instead of going to deep water
It was calling loudly for help from nearby boats
It was following their boat closely out of curiosity
It jumped out of the water many times to show off
questions.why: The story says the whale kept swimming in circles instead of heading out to the deep sea.

wrong.B: The story does not say the whale called loudly.
wrong.C: The story does not say the whale followed the boat.
wrong.D: The story does not mention the whale jumping.

questions.stem: In the story, a pod is —
options: a kind of boat
a group of whales
a deep hole in the sea
a loud whale sound
questions.why: The story says a pod is the group of whales the young whale normally travels with.

wrong.A: A pod is not a boat.
wrong.C: A pod is not a hole in the sea.
wrong.D: A pod is not a sound.

questions.stem: Why didn't the team touch the whale or make loud noise?
options: Touching whales is against the law in every country
Loud noise or touching could scare the whale further
The whale might bite them if they got too close
The water was too shallow to get close to the whale

wrong.A: The story never mentions a law.
wrong.C: The story does not say the whale might bite anyone.
wrong.D: The story does not give this as the reason.

questions.stem: Why did the team make a slow, steady sound instead of staying silent?
options: To call other fishermen for help
To scare the whale away from the shore with loud noises
To calmly guide the whale toward deep water
To test their boat's engine
questions.why: The steady sound was used to calmly lead the whale toward the deep sea, not to scare it or test equipment.

wrong.A: The sound was meant for the whale, not other fishermen.
wrong.B: Scaring the whale could make things worse, which is the opposite of the goal.
wrong.D: Testing the engine was not the purpose.

questions.stem: What happened right after the fishermen saw the whale?
options: The whale found its pod and swam away from the beach
The children went swimming near the boat in the bay
The fishermen called for help from biologists
The whale swam into deep water by itself at night

wrong.A: This happens near the very end of the story.
wrong.B: The children never go swimming in the story.
wrong.D: This also happens later, after help arrives.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us the children watched quietly and stayed calm?
options: To show that watching whales is boring for the children all day
To show that staying calm and patient helps a frightened animal
To explain how to build a boat out of wood and rope
To show that the children were tired and sleepy at night
questions.why: The children's calm, quiet behavior supports the story's lesson that patience helps a frightened animal feel safe.

wrong.A: Nothing suggests the children were bored.
wrong.C: The story is not about building boats.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests the children were tired.

LOW.prompt: Do you think the fishermen and children did the right thing by using a slow, steady sound instead of touching the whale? Use at least two facts from the story to explain your answer.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think they did the right thing. The story says loud noise or touching could scare the whale even more. It also says the slow, steady sound helped guide the whale back to the deep sea, where it found its pod again.

keyWords.definition: a steady flow of water moving in one direction
keyWords.example: The strong current carried the boat downstream.

keyWords.definition: unable to think clearly or know what to do
keyWords.example: The lost tourist looked confused at the map.

keyWords.definition: careful study done to learn new facts about something
keyWords.example: The scientist's research taught us about bird migration.

keyWords.definition: the ability to stay calm while waiting or working slowly
keyWords.example: Growing a garden takes a lot of patience.

keyWords.definition: the edge of the land where it meets the sea
keyWords.example: Fishing villages dot the long coastline.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Whales swim in circles close to the shore without ever needing any help from people from fishermen or from scientists.
Children are kept far away from whales during rescues like this one.
Research centers in this coastal area study fish more than whales.
Fishermen and biologists work together with patience to guide a confused young whale back to open water.
questions.why: The article describes fishermen, biologists, and children working patiently together to guide a confused young whale to safety.

wrong.A: The article does not say whales always circle near shore; this whale was lost.
wrong.B: Children were present and helped by observing calmly.
wrong.C: The research center clearly studies whales in this article.

questions.stem: What does Dr. Huda say can separate a young whale from its pod?
options: A strong current or the noise of passing boats
A lack of food in the bay near the shore
Another, older whale chasing it away from the pod
A storm far out at sea that frightened it
questions.why: Dr. Huda explains that a strong current or the noise of passing boats can separate a young whale from its pod.

wrong.B: The article does not mention a lack of food.
wrong.C: The article does not mention another whale chasing it.
wrong.D: The article does not mention a storm.

questions.stem: What method does the team use to guide the whale?
options: They tow the whale slowly back to sea with a long rope
They use the boats engine to make a slow, steady sound
They throw fresh fish into the deep water nearby
They swim closely next to the whale the whole time
questions.why: The article describes the team using the boat's engine to create a slow, steady sound to guide the whale.

wrong.A: The article does not describe towing the whale.
wrong.C: The article does not mention throwing fish.
wrong.D: The article does not describe anyone swimming next to the whale.

questions.stem: In the article, the word confused means —
options: excited and happy about the road ahead of them today
unable to think clearly about which way to go
very hungry and thirsty after the trip
fast and strong enough to run far away from the camp
questions.why: The confused whale did not know which way the open sea lay and kept circling.

wrong.A: Confused does not mean excited and happy.
wrong.C: Confused does not mean hungry.
wrong.D: Confused does not mean fast and strong.

questions.stem: What might happen if the team used sudden, loud noise near the whale?
options: The whale would immediately find its pod and swim home
The whale might panic and swim farther into danger
The whale would fall asleep and drift to the beach
The tide would rise faster and push it out to sea
questions.why: A frightened whale might panic and swim even farther into danger, so loud noise is avoided.

wrong.A: Loud noise would not help the whale find its pod.
wrong.C: The article never suggests the whale would fall asleep.
wrong.D: Noise has no effect on the tide.

questions.stem: Why were the schoolchildren allowed to be so close to this rescue?
options: They happened to already be on the biologists' research boat for a field trip
They were trained lifeguards who worked at the beach near the harbor every day
They asked the fishermen for a ride out to the whale after school
They were the whale's owners and had cared for it since it was small
questions.why: The article says the children were already aboard the biologists' research boat on a field trip when the rescue began.

wrong.B: The article never calls the children lifeguards.
wrong.C: The article does not say they asked for a ride.
wrong.D: Wild whales do not have owners.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: (1) Dr. Huda explains why the whale is confused, (2) the fishermen spot the whale, (3) the whale rejoins its pod, (4) the team makes a steady sound.
questions.why: The fishermen spot the whale first, Dr. Huda then explains the confusion, the team makes the steady sound, and finally the whale rejoins its pod.

wrong.B: The fishermen must spot the whale before anything else happens.
wrong.C: The whale cannot rejoin its pod before the rescue even begins.
wrong.D: The explanation comes before the sound is made, not after.

questions.stem: How are the fishermen's and the biologists' roles different in this rescue?
options: The fishermen cared for the whale's health, while the biologists caught fish for it to eat after the rescue is done
The fishermen first noticed and reported the whale, while the biologists understood whale behavior and guided it to safety
The fishermen and biologists did exactly the same job all day long, with no difference between them
The biologists caught the whale in a net while the fishermen watched from the beach and took some photos
questions.why: The fishermen spotted and reported the whale, while the biologists used their scientific knowledge to guide it safely back to sea.

wrong.A: The fishermen did not care for the whale's health, and the biologists did not catch fish.
wrong.C: Their roles were different, not the same.
wrong.D: No net was used in the rescue.

MID.prompt: Explain how teamwork and patience helped guide the lost whale back to the open sea. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Teamwork and patience worked together to help the whale. The fishermen spotted the confused whale and quickly called the coastal research center, while Dr. Huda and her team understood that young whales can lose their pod and should not be frightened with noise. By using a slow, steady sound from their engine, the team patiently guided the whale toward deep water until it finally rejoined its pod.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies living things
keyWords.example: A biologist spent years studying coral reefs.

keyWords.definition: relating to sound or the sense of hearing
keyWords.example: The hall was designed with excellent acoustic quality for concerts.

keyWords.definition: to find and follow a path or direction, especially when traveling
keyWords.example: Sailors once used the stars to navigate across the ocean.

keyWords.definition: to save someone or something from danger
keyWords.example: Firefighters organized a daring rescue after the flood.

keyWords.definition: to move from one place to another, often with the seasons
keyWords.example: Many birds migrate south before winter arrives.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Humpback whales never travel in any groups and migrate alone across the ocean.
The Red Sea coast is too dangerous for research boats to work near it.
Marine biologists regularly capture wild whales so they can study them closely inside large tanks.
A young, disoriented whale is guided back to open water by fishermen, biologists, and schoolchildren.
questions.why: The article describes fishermen, biologists, and schoolchildren combining patience and knowledge to guide a disoriented whale back to open water.

wrong.A: In the article, whales normally travel with a pod, a group.
wrong.B: The article shows research boats operating safely along the coast.
wrong.C: The whale is guided back to the sea, not captured.

questions.stem: According to the article, what can cause a young whale to become separated from its pod?
options: A strong current or the noise of passing vessels
A lack of sunlight during the day near the coast
Too much food near the coastline close to shore
Competing with other whales for territory nearby
questions.why: The article explicitly states that a strong current or the noise of passing vessels can separate a young whale from its pod.

wrong.B: Sunlight is not mentioned as a cause.
wrong.C: Food supply is not mentioned as a cause.
wrong.D: Territory competition is not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: What specific technique does Dr. Huda's team use to guide the whale, and why?
options: They play recorded dolphin sounds because the whales are afraid of dolphins and swim away fast
They create a slow, steady acoustic signal because whales find it calming rather than threatening
They flash bright lights across the water to try to lead the whale forward in the dark
They release food into the water to try to lure the whale forward, since it is hungry
questions.why: In the article, the team used the boat's engine to produce a slow, steady acoustic signal that whales find calming rather than threatening.

wrong.A: The article never mentions dolphin sounds or whales fearing dolphins.
wrong.C: The article does not mention lights.
wrong.D: The article does not mention luring the whale with food.

questions.stem: In the article, the word navigate most nearly means —
options: to find and follow a path or direction
to make a very loud noise at night
to search for food in the hot forest
to swim backward across the lake
questions.why: The whale could not navigate, meaning it could not find its way, back toward deeper water.

wrong.B: Navigate does not mean making noise.
wrong.C: Navigate does not mean searching for food.
wrong.D: Navigate does not mean swimming backward.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that humpback whales migrate long distances each year?
options: To explain why the whale was likely traveling along a migration route when it became separated from its pod
To prove that humpback whales never stay near the Red Sea, and only live in cold places far away from it
To show that whales migrate once in their lives, so the whale was probably on its first trip
To explain why fishermen rarely find whales in the sea, since the animals swim too fast for boats
questions.why: Mentioning the whale's long seasonal migration helps explain how it ended up near this coastline while traveling with, and then losing, its pod.

wrong.B: The whale passes close to the coast.
wrong.C: The article implies migration happens regularly, not just once.
wrong.D: The fishermen did find a whale in this story.

questions.stem: Which correctly orders these events?
options: Whale rejoins pod → fishermen spot whale → team uses acoustic signal → biologists arrive
Fishermen spot whale → biologists arrive → team uses acoustic signal → whale rejoins pod
Biologists arrive → whale rejoins pod → fishermen spot whale → team uses acoustic signal
Team uses acoustic signal → fishermen spot whale → biologists arrive → whale rejoins pod
questions.why: The fishermen spot the whale first, the biologists arrive next, the team then uses the acoustic signal, and the whale finally rejoins its pod.

wrong.A: The whale cannot rejoin its pod before the rescue even starts.
wrong.C: Biologists cannot arrive before the whale is even spotted.
wrong.D: The acoustic signal is used after the biologists arrive, not before the whale is spotted.

questions.stem: How does the biologists' approach to this rescue differ from simply chasing the whale toward open water?
options: It relies on patient, calming sound rather than force or sudden noise that could frighten the whale further
It involves capturing the whale with strong nets so that it can be carried to the open sea by a big truck
It requires no understanding of whale behavior, only strong boats and a lot of speed
It is the same as chasing the whale, but slower and with a few more boats
questions.why: Rather than forcing or chasing the whale, the biologists used a calm, steady sound based on an understanding of whale behavior.

wrong.B: No nets are used in this rescue.
wrong.C: The approach depends heavily on knowledge of whale behavior.
wrong.D: Chasing would risk frightening the whale, which is the opposite of this calm method.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that the biologists later used the event to train future rescues and keep long-term records?
options: To suggest that such rescues are rare, pointless events that scientists do not remember
To show that careful observation and documentation help improve future wildlife rescues
To criticize the fishermen for calling for help instead of leaving the whale alone
To argue that whales should be kept away from research boats and from all people
questions.why: Mentioning the long-term records and training shows how careful documentation of this rescue can help future wildlife rescues succeed.

wrong.A: The article treats the rescue as meaningful, not pointless.
wrong.C: The fishermen's call for help was essential, not criticized.
wrong.D: The research boat's presence helped, rather than harmed, the whale.

HIGH.prompt: The article shows a rescue based on patience and scientific understanding rather than quick, forceful action. Do you think this approach is the best way to help wildlife in distress? Support your argument with evidence from the article, and address a point someone might raise against your view.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed a point against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that patience and scientific understanding are the best way to help wildlife in distress. The article shows that touching the whale or making sudden loud noise could have caused it to panic and swim further into danger, while a slow, steady acoustic signal calmly guided it back to open water. Someone might argue that a faster, more forceful rescue would have saved time, but the article shows that forcing a frightened animal often makes a dangerous situation worse, so the patient approach used by Dr. Huda's team was clearly the safer and more effective choice.

LOW.stem: Where was the whale at the start of the story?
options: In shallow water
Far out at sea
In a big river
Under the ice
LOW.why: In the story, the whale was in shallow water near the shore.

wrong.B: It needed help to get back to deep water.
wrong.C: It was in the sea, not a river.
wrong.D: There is no ice in the story.

LOW.stem: Why was the whale alone in the bay?
options: It wanted to play with the kids.
It was looking for some fish.
It had lost its pod.
It liked the shallow water.
LOW.why: In the text, the whale had lost its group, and a group of whales is a pod.

wrong.A: The kids came later to learn.
wrong.B: Fish are not mentioned.
wrong.D: Swimming in rings shows it was lost, not that it liked the water.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does the word "guide" mean?
options: Scare away
Wake up
Hold tight
Show the way
LOW.why: The soft sound guided the whale, and the whale swam after the boat toward the sea.

wrong.A: The team did not want to scare the whale.
wrong.B: The sound was not meant to wake it.
wrong.C: No one touched the whale.

LOW.stem: What did the other whales do when the whale swam out to sea?
options: They swam away fast.
They called to it.
They hid under the boat.
They splashed the kids.
LOW.why: The text says other whales called to it and the whale found its pod.

wrong.A: The whales welcomed it; they did not swim away.
wrong.C: No whales hid under the boat.
wrong.D: The kids were not splashed.

MID.stem: What did the fishermen think might happen if the tide dropped?
options: The whale might join its pod.
The whale might get stuck.
The whale might jump out of the water.
The whale might sink the boat.
MID.why: The fishermen worried the whale might get stuck if the tide dropped.

wrong.A: The text does not link the tide to the pod.
wrong.C: Jumping is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The boat is not mentioned as being in danger.

MID.stem: In the article, what does the word "shallow" mean?
options: Very cold and dark
Full of fish and boats
Not deep
Far from the shore
MID.why: The whale circled in shallow water near the shoreline instead of heading to open water, so shallow means not deep.

wrong.A: Temperature is not mentioned.
wrong.B: The text does not say the water was full of fish.
wrong.D: The whale was near the shoreline, not far from it.

MID.stem: What can you infer from the other whales calling back at the end?
options: The pod was angry that it left
The boat had scared the pod
The young whale was lost again
The pod was answering it
MID.why: The whales called back and the young whale rejoined its pod, so they were answering it.

wrong.A: The text gives no sign of anger.
wrong.B: The boat had helped guide the whale.
wrong.C: The whale had reached open sea and rejoined the pod.

MID.stem: How long did the rescue take before the whale reached the open sea?
options: Nearly an hour
A few short minutes
All day long
Two whole days
MID.why: The text says the whale reached the open sea after nearly an hour.

wrong.B: Minutes is how long it took for the helpers to set out.
wrong.C: The rescue took about an hour, not all day.
wrong.D: Two days is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: In the article, what does the word "disoriented" mean?
options: Very hungry and weak
Angry at the boat
Unsure which way to go
Proud and strong
HIGH.why: The whale kept turning in one narrow stretch and could not find its way to deeper water, so it was unsure of direction.

wrong.A: Hunger is not mentioned.
wrong.B: The whale is not described as angry.
wrong.D: The whale was lost and in need of help.

HIGH.stem: About how old did the fishermen think the whale was?
options: About ten or twelve years old
Only a few days or weeks old
More than twenty years old
No more than a year or two old
HIGH.why: Judging by its size, the fishermen guessed it was no more than a year or two old.

wrong.A: The fishermen thought it was a young whale.
wrong.B: They did not say it was only days old.
wrong.C: They thought it was young, not twenty.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author explain what a pod does for young whales?
options: To show why a lone young whale was in trouble
To explain how the fishermen spotted it
To show how biologists train for rescues
To describe the songs whales sing at sea
HIGH.why: The pod guides young whales during long journeys, so being separated leaves the whale unable to navigate.

wrong.B: The fishermen spotted it by chance near the shoreline.
wrong.C: Training is not part of this explanation.
wrong.D: The explanation is about guidance, not songs.

HIGH.stem: Why did Captain Yusuf radio the research center instead of trying to rescue the whale himself?
options: His own boat was too small to move
He knew trained experts could help safely
He wanted the schoolchildren to join him
The research center owned the whale
HIGH.why: He called for a rescue team of marine biologists, who know how to help lost whales.

wrong.A: The size of his boat is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The children happened to be aboard the biologists' boat.
wrong.D: No one owns the whale in the article.
